options.a: Pure death benefit coverage for a specified period without cash value
options.b: Level lifetime death benefit with a scheduled cash value buildup
options.c: Death benefit for a set period that builds cash value after year three
options.d: Flexible premiums and an adjustable death benefit with a cash account

distractorExplanations.b: This describes whole life (permanent coverage with guaranteed cash values), not term's temporary protection with no cash value.
distractorExplanations.c: Term insurance never accumulates cash value at any point; cash value is a feature of permanent policies only.
distractorExplanations.d: Flexible premiums, adjustable face amount, and a cash account describe universal life, not term insurance.

options.a: Provides coverage for a set term that can be renewed without evidence
options.b: Combines permanent death benefit with cash value accumulation
options.c: Lets the owner skip premiums and adjust the face amount at will
options.d: Invests cash value in separate accounts chosen by the policyowner

distractorExplanations.a: Renewal without evidence of insurability describes renewable term, which is temporary; whole life is permanent with cash value.
distractorExplanations.c: Flexible premiums and an adjustable face amount are universal life features; whole life has fixed level premiums.
distractorExplanations.d: Separate-account subaccounts describe variable life; traditional whole life cash value grows at a guaranteed rate in the general account.

options.a: The policy owner/beneficiary and the insured at the time of the claim
options.b: The insurer and the insured at each annual policy anniversary date
options.c: The producer and the applicant when the application is signed
options.d: The policy owner/beneficiary and the insured at policy inception

distractorExplanations.a: Insurable interest for life insurance is required at inception, not at death or claim; the at-loss timing is the property insurance rule.
distractorExplanations.b: The required relationship is owner/beneficiary to insured, not insurer to insured, and it is not re-tested at each anniversary.
distractorExplanations.c: The agent has no insurable interest in the applicant's life; the relationship must exist between owner/beneficiary and insured.

options.a: Insurer's ability to contest the policy after it has been in force ~2 years
options.b: Policyowner's right to return the policy for a full refund after 10 days
options.c: Insured's ability to change beneficiaries after the policy is 2 years old
options.d: Insurer's ability to adjust the benefit for a misstated age after 2 years

distractorExplanations.b: Returning the policy for a full refund within a set window is the free-look provision, not the incontestability clause.
distractorExplanations.c: Beneficiary changes depend on revocable or irrevocable designation; incontestability limits the insurer, not the owner, and has no such bar.
distractorExplanations.d: Misstatement of age is not barred by incontestability; the insurer can adjust the benefit to what the premium would have bought at the correct age.

options.a: Fixed level premiums and a set face amount with cash value
options.b: Flexible premiums and adjustable death benefit with cash value
options.c: Level premiums for a set term with a conversion option to whole life
options.d: Decreasing death benefit over a set term to match a mortgage balance

distractorExplanations.a: Fixed level premiums with a set face amount describe traditional whole life, not universal life's flexible design.
distractorExplanations.c: A level-premium term with a conversion privilege is convertible term; universal life is permanent with a cash value account.
distractorExplanations.d: A death benefit that declines with a loan balance is decreasing (mortgage) term, not permanent universal life with cash value.

life-health-insurance-readiness-check-li.explanation: UL separates insurance cost from cash value with flexibility. Cash value earns current crediting rates subject to a guaranteed minimum.

options.a: Total of final expenses, debts, and education funds the family needs
options.b: Face amount equal to ten times the insured's current annual salary
options.c: Present value of future earnings the family would lose
options.d: Cash value already built in existing policies

distractorExplanations.a: Totaling specific family needs (final expenses, debts, education) is the needs approach, not the Human Life Value approach.
distractorExplanations.b: A salary multiple is a rule of thumb; Human Life Value discounts the insured's future earnings net of personal consumption.
distractorExplanations.d: Existing cash value is an asset that offsets need; it is not the economic value of the earnings the family would lose.

options.a: Higher premiums for the first years that then drop to a lower level
options.b: Level premiums with a death benefit that increases each year
options.c: Limited benefits in the first two or three years then full coverage
options.d: Lower initial premiums that increase for a period then level off

distractorExplanations.a: This reverses the graded pattern; a graded premium policy starts with lower premiums that rise, not higher premiums that fall.
distractorExplanations.b: An increasing death benefit with level premiums describes an increasing-benefit design, not a graded premium schedule.
distractorExplanations.c: Reduced early benefits describe a graded death benefit (often guaranteed-issue) policy, a different product from graded premium.

options.a: Ownership rights (and sometimes beneficiary) to another party
options.b: The insured's status as the person whose life is covered
options.c: The insurer's obligation under the policy to a reinsurer
options.d: Only the right to name beneficiaries, with ownership unchanged

distractorExplanations.b: Assignment cannot change who the insured is; it transfers the owner's rights (absolutely or as collateral) to another party.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving part of the insurer's risk to a reinsurer is reinsurance cession, not an owner's assignment of policy rights.
distractorExplanations.d: Naming beneficiaries is a separate ownership right; assignment transfers ownership (absolute) or a security interest (collateral).

options.a: Excludes suicide for the policy's lifetime, refunding premiums paid
options.b: Bars the insurer from contesting misstatements after two years
options.c: Limits death benefit if suicide occurs within first 1-2 years
options.d: Limits the benefit only if suicide occurs within the first 5 years

distractorExplanations.a: The suicide exclusion lasts only the first one to two years; after that period, suicide is a covered cause of death.
distractorExplanations.b: Barring contests of application misstatements after two years is the incontestable clause, not the suicide clause.
distractorExplanations.d: The typical suicide exclusion period is one to two years (two in most states), not five years.

options.a: Dividends to buy one-year term insurance equal to the cash value
options.b: Dividends to reduce the next annual premium due on the policy
options.c: Cash value to purchase a smaller paid-up policy after lapse
options.d: Dividends to purchase additional paid-up whole life insurance

distractorExplanations.a: Using dividends for one-year term coverage is the one-year term dividend option, not the paid-up additions rider.
distractorExplanations.b: Applying dividends against the next premium is the premium-reduction dividend option, not paid-up additions.
distractorExplanations.c: Using cash value for a smaller paid-up policy is the reduced paid-up nonforfeiture option, which uses cash value rather than dividends.

options.a: Income tax-free to the beneficiary
options.b: Taxed as ordinary income
options.c: Taxed as capital gains above premiums paid
options.d: Tax-free only if paid in installments

distractorExplanations.b: Lump-sum death proceeds are excluded from income under IRC 101(a); only interest earned on installment payouts is taxable.
distractorExplanations.c: Taxing the gain over premiums paid is the rule for cash value surrenders, not for death proceeds paid to a beneficiary.
distractorExplanations.d: This reverses the rule: a lump sum is tax-free, while the interest portion of installment payouts is taxable.

life-health-insurance-readiness-check-li.explanation: IRC §101(a) generally excludes death proceeds from income tax. Estate tax may still apply if the insured's estate owned the policy.

options.a: Stopping premiums while keeping the full face as term for a period
options.b: Stopping premiums while keeping reduced permanent death benefit
options.c: Taking the cash surrender value and ending all coverage
options.d: Using the cash value to pay overdue premiums as a policy loan

distractorExplanations.a: Keeping the full face amount as term for a limited period is the extended term option, not reduced paid-up.
distractorExplanations.c: Taking the cash value and ending coverage is the cash surrender option; reduced paid-up keeps a smaller permanent policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Paying overdue premiums by loan against cash value is the automatic premium loan provision, which keeps the original face amount.

options.a: The first of two insureds dies
options.b: Either insured becomes disabled
options.c: The second of two insureds dies
options.d: Both insureds reach age 100

distractorExplanations.a: Paying at the first death describes a first-to-die joint life policy, not survivorship (second-to-die) coverage.
distractorExplanations.b: Survivorship life pays on death, not disability; disability protection comes from a waiver of premium rider or DI coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: Reaching a maturity age triggers endowment or policy maturity, not the survivorship death benefit.

life-health-insurance-readiness-check-li.explanation: Survivorship policy funds estate tax at second death. It is often used in estate planning to fund estate taxes due at the second death.

options.a: Use of any provider with lower cost sharing for in-network care
options.b: Payment of a deductible before any preventive visit is covered
options.c: Filing claim forms for reimbursement after paying providers in full
options.d: Selection of a primary care physician and referrals for specialists

distractorExplanations.a: Freedom to use any provider with better in-network cost sharing describes a PPO, not an HMO's gatekeeper model.
distractorExplanations.b: HMOs cover preventive care with little or no cost sharing, and the ACA requires in-network preventive care without a deductible.
distractorExplanations.c: Paying providers and filing for reimbursement describes indemnity plans; HMO members pay copays and providers bill the HMO.

options.a: Ambulatory, emergency, hospitalization, maternity, mental health, and prescriptions
options.b: Ambulatory, emergency, hospitalization, adult dental, adult vision, and long-term care
options.c: Emergency, hospitalization, cosmetic surgery, and nonprescription weight-loss drugs
options.d: Hospitalization and prescriptions only, with maternity as an optional rider

distractorExplanations.b: Adult dental, adult vision, and long-term care are not essential health benefits; only pediatric dental and vision are.
distractorExplanations.c: Cosmetic procedures and over-the-counter weight-loss drugs are excluded from the ten essential health benefit categories.
distractorExplanations.d: Maternity and newborn care is a required EHB category under the ACA, not an optional rider.

life-health-insurance-readiness-check-he.explanation: EHB categories must be covered in individual/small group ACA plans. Preventive services, rehabilitative care, lab services, and pediatric care are also EHB categories.

options.a: Former employees to convert group life coverage to individual policies
options.b: Former employees to keep group health coverage temporarily
options.c: Laid-off workers to keep coverage at the employer's contribution rate
options.d: Former employees to keep group health coverage for up to 60 months

distractorExplanations.a: Converting group life to an individual policy is the group life conversion privilege, not COBRA health continuation.
distractorExplanations.c: COBRA enrollees may be charged up to 102% of the total premium; the employer is not required to keep subsidizing coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: COBRA lasts 18 months for job loss (29 with disability, 36 for some dependent events), not 60 months.

life-health-insurance-readiness-check-he.explanation: COBRA extends group coverage 18-36 months typically at employee cost. The qualified beneficiary may be charged up to 102% of the full premium.

options.a: Requiring a PCP referral before any out-of-network care is covered
options.b: Covering out-of-network care only in emergencies but with no referrals
options.c: Allowing out-of-network care at higher cost sharing without PCP gatekeeper
options.d: Paying providers a fixed monthly capitation fee for each member enrolled

distractorExplanations.a: Requiring a PCP referral for out-of-network benefits describes a point-of-service (POS) plan, not a PPO.
distractorExplanations.b: Emergency-only out-of-network coverage without referrals describes an EPO; a PPO pays out-of-network care at higher cost sharing.
distractorExplanations.d: Capitation is the classic HMO payment model; PPOs pay network providers discounted fee-for-service rates.

life-health-insurance-readiness-check-he.explanation: PPOs offer flexibility with network discounts and OON option. PPOs typically need no PCP referral for specialists.

options.a: Prescription drug coverage through private plans
options.b: Physician and outpatient services through Original Medicare
options.c: Inpatient hospital and hospice coverage
options.d: Private plans bundling Parts A and B, usually with drugs

distractorExplanations.b: Physician and outpatient services are Medicare Part B, not Part D prescription drug coverage.
distractorExplanations.c: Inpatient hospital and hospice care are Medicare Part A benefits, not Part D drug coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: Private plans that bundle Parts A and B are Medicare Advantage (Part C); Part D is the standalone drug benefit.

options.a: Fixed dollar amount the insured pays for each office visit
options.b: Amount the insured pays before plan begins sharing costs
options.c: Most the insured pays in covered costs in a plan year
options.d: Percentage of covered costs the insured pays after the plan starts paying

distractorExplanations.a: A fixed dollar amount per visit is a copayment, not the deductible that must be met before cost sharing begins.
distractorExplanations.c: The cap on what the insured pays in a year is the out-of-pocket maximum, not the deductible.
distractorExplanations.d: A percentage share paid after the deductible is coinsurance, not the deductible itself.

options.a: Pre-tax contributions that are forfeited if unspent by plan year-end
options.b: Tax-free employer reimbursements with funds owned by the employer
options.c: Deductible contributions, tax-free growth, tax-free qualified medical withdrawals
options.d: Deductible contributions with any health plan, plus tax-free medical withdrawals

distractorExplanations.a: The use-it-or-lose-it rule applies to health FSAs; HSA balances roll over year to year and stay with the owner.
distractorExplanations.b: Employer-funded, employer-owned reimbursement accounts are HRAs; an HSA is owned by the individual.
distractorExplanations.d: HSA contributions require enrollment in a qualifying high-deductible health plan, not any plan.

life-health-insurance-readiness-check-he.explanation: HSA tax benefits require qualifying HDHP. Together these form the HSA's triple tax advantage.

options.a: Are limited to 12 months after enrollment for adult applicants
options.b: Are allowed only if the applicant had a coverage gap over 63 days
options.c: Are prohibited for children under 19 but allowed for adults
options.d: Are prohibited for plan years beginning on/after 2014

distractorExplanations.a: The 12-month exclusion limit was the pre-ACA HIPAA group-plan rule; the ACA eliminated these exclusions from 2014.
distractorExplanations.b: The 63-day break-in-coverage test was a HIPAA creditable-coverage rule that no longer applies after the ACA.
distractorExplanations.c: The under-19 protection was the 2010 interim rule; from 2014 the ban extended to applicants of all ages.

life-health-insurance-readiness-check-he.explanation: ACA banned pre-existing condition exclusions in individual/small group. The ban applies in ACA-compliant individual and small-group markets.

options.a: Employer against catastrophic claim levels above specified thresholds
options.b: Employees against out-of-pocket costs above the plan's annual maximum
options.c: Plan participants if the employer becomes insolvent and stops paying
options.d: Insurer against catastrophic losses it cedes under a treaty contract

distractorExplanations.b: The out-of-pocket maximum is plan design that protects employees; stop-loss reimburses the self-funded employer.
distractorExplanations.c: Stop-loss is a contract with the employer, not a guarantee to participants if the employer fails.
distractorExplanations.d: Ceding losses under a treaty is reinsurance of an insurer; stop-loss protects a self-funded employer plan.

options.a: Federal program for people 65+ and certain disabled individuals
options.b: Joint federal-state program for low-income eligible individuals
options.c: Private supplemental policy filling Medicare's cost-sharing gaps
options.d: State-run program covering workers injured on the job

distractorExplanations.a: A federal program for people 65 and older and certain disabled people is Medicare, not Medicaid.
distractorExplanations.c: A private policy that fills Medicare cost-sharing gaps is Medigap (Medicare Supplement), not Medicaid.
distractorExplanations.d: Coverage for on-the-job injuries is workers' compensation, not the means-tested Medicaid program.

options.a: Order in which multiple beneficiaries receive life insurance proceeds
options.b: How a plan recovers costs from a third party who caused the injury
options.c: Which plan pays first when insured has multiple coverages
options.d: How costs split after the deductible

distractorExplanations.a: The order of life insurance payees is set by primary and contingent beneficiary designations, not coordination of benefits.
distractorExplanations.b: Recovering costs from a liable third party is subrogation, not coordination of benefits between two plans.
distractorExplanations.d: The cost split after the deductible is coinsurance; COB decides which of two plans is primary.

options.a: Payment for each service billed at a negotiated discounted fee
options.b: Fixed payment per hospital stay based on the diagnosis group
options.c: Bonus payments tied to quality and cost targets per year
options.d: Fixed per-member payment regardless of services rendered

distractorExplanations.a: Paying per service at a negotiated discount is discounted fee-for-service (the PPO model), not capitation.
distractorExplanations.b: A fixed payment per admission based on diagnosis is a DRG case rate, not a per-member capitation payment.
distractorExplanations.c: Bonuses for hitting quality and cost targets describe pay-for-performance, not fixed per-member capitation.

options.a: A deductible measured in days before benefits begin
options.b: A grace period of days after a missed premium is due
options.c: A probationary period before illness is covered under a new policy
options.d: A coinsurance percentage paid after benefits begin

distractorExplanations.b: A grace period keeps coverage in force after a missed premium; it does not delay when benefits begin.
distractorExplanations.c: A probationary period runs once from policy issue for sickness; the elimination period applies to each claim like a deductible.
distractorExplanations.d: Coinsurance is a percentage share after benefits start, not a waiting period measured in days before benefits begin.

options.a: Let employees keep group health coverage after leaving by paying the premium
options.b: Limit exclusion periods for pre-existing conditions when changing group coverage
options.c: Protect the privacy of individually identifiable health information
options.d: Prohibit pre-existing condition exclusions in every individual market policy

distractorExplanations.a: Keeping group coverage after leaving a job by paying the premium is COBRA continuation, not HIPAA portability.
distractorExplanations.c: Health information privacy is the HIPAA Privacy Rule (administrative simplification), not the Title I portability provisions.
distractorExplanations.d: Banning exclusions in individual policies came with the ACA in 2014; HIPAA only limited exclusion periods in group plans.

options.a: Adhesion, so ambiguities are construed in the insurer's favor
options.b: Indemnity, so life insurance pays only the actual loss
options.c: Utmost good faith requiring full disclosure
options.d: Aleatory exchange requiring equal values from both parties

distractorExplanations.a: Insurance is a contract of adhesion, but ambiguities are construed against the insurer that drafted it, not in its favor.
distractorExplanations.b: Life insurance is a valued contract paying the face amount; the indemnity principle applies to property coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: Aleatory means an unequal exchange of values; an equal exchange describes a commutative contract.

options.a: Insured recovers the policy's face amount even if the loss is smaller
options.b: Insurer takes over the insured's rights against a negligent third party
options.c: Insured must have a financial stake in the property at policy issue
options.d: Insured should not profit from a loss beyond actual financial loss

distractorExplanations.a: Paying the stated amount regardless of the actual loss describes a valued policy, which is the opposite of indemnity.
distractorExplanations.b: Taking over the insured's recovery rights is subrogation, which supports indemnity but is a separate principle.
distractorExplanations.c: Requiring a financial stake in the property is insurable interest, not the principle of indemnity.

options.a: Are strictly complied with; breach may void coverage regardless of materiality
options.b: Are statements the applicant believes true to the best of their knowledge
options.c: Are binding only if the false statement was material to the risk
options.d: Are promises the insurer makes about future dividend payments

distractorExplanations.b: Statements believed true to the best of the applicant's knowledge are representations, not warranties.
distractorExplanations.c: The materiality requirement applies to representations; a warranty breach historically voids coverage without proof of materiality.
distractorExplanations.d: Warranties are statements or promises by the insured about facts or conditions; dividends are not guaranteed by any warranty.

options.a: Coverage may begin on the receipt date if the applicant is later found insurable
options.b: Coverage begins immediately and stays in force even if underwriting declines
options.c: Coverage begins only on policy delivery once the first premium is collected
options.d: Coverage begins on the receipt date unless the agent later rejects the risk

distractorExplanations.b: No receipt keeps coverage after a decline; even a binding receipt ends interim coverage once the insurer declines.
distractorExplanations.c: Delivery-date coverage is the rule when no premium is paid with the application; a conditional receipt can make coverage retroactive.
distractorExplanations.d: Underwriting decisions belong to the insurer, not the agent; the condition is the applicant's insurability.

life-health-insurance-readiness-check-la.explanation: Life producers use conditional or binding receipts for the gap after application and premium. This is not a property-casualty auto or homeowners binder. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not a state insurance exam paper. The condition is that the applicant was insurable as applied for.

options.a: Requiring insurers to send every applicant a free copy of their full credit report
options.b: Making the insurer, not the reporting agency, correct disputed report entries
options.c: Letting insurers keep adverse items on a consumer's report indefinitely
options.d: Requiring adverse action notices if credit-based decisions negatively impact consumer

distractorExplanations.a: FCRA requires disclosure and a free-report right after adverse action, not a credit report mailed to every applicant.
distractorExplanations.b: Disputed report entries are investigated and corrected by the consumer reporting agency, not by the insurer.
distractorExplanations.c: FCRA limits most negative items to seven years (ten for bankruptcy); reports cannot carry them indefinitely.

options.a: Disclosure forms comparing existing and proposed coverage
options.b: Written consent from the existing insurer before the new policy issues
options.c: Surrender of the old policy before the new application is signed
options.d: A signed statement only if the new policy has a lower premium

distractorExplanations.b: The existing insurer must be notified of the replacement, but its consent is not required.
distractorExplanations.c: Surrendering the old policy first is what replacement rules warn against, since it can leave the client uninsured.
distractorExplanations.d: Replacement disclosure applies to any replacement, not just when the new policy costs less.

life-health-insurance-readiness-check-la.explanation: Replacement regulations protect consumers from unnecessary churn. State replacement regulations set the required forms and notices.

options.a: Oral statements made by the agent at the sale override the written policy
options.b: Written contract terms generally cannot be contradicted by prior oral agreements
options.c: Ambiguous policy wording is interpreted in favor of the insured party
options.d: A party who knowingly gives up a known right cannot later reclaim it

distractorExplanations.a: This reverses the rule; the parol evidence rule keeps prior oral statements from changing the written contract.
distractorExplanations.c: Construing ambiguity for the insured is the adhesion (contra proferentem) doctrine, not the parol evidence rule.
distractorExplanations.d: Voluntarily giving up a known right is waiver, a separate doctrine from the parol evidence rule.

options.a: Making false statements about a competitor's financial condition
options.b: Offering an inducement not stated in the policy to buy coverage
options.c: Inducing replacement of a policy by misrepresentation or incomplete comparison
options.d: Misrepresenting a policy's terms, benefits, or dividends to make a sale

distractorExplanations.a: False statements about a competitor's finances are defamation of an insurer, not twisting a policyowner into replacement.
distractorExplanations.b: Offering an inducement not in the policy is rebating; twisting is inducing a replacement through misrepresentation.
distractorExplanations.d: This is general misrepresentation; twisting specifically means using misrepresentation to induce a policy replacement.

options.a: Paying policy dividends as a return of excess premium to owners
options.b: Sharing commissions with an unlicensed person who referred the client
options.c: Inducing a policyowner to replace coverage through misrepresentation
options.d: Returning premium or giving inducement not specified in the policy

distractorExplanations.a: Dividends are a contractual return of excess premium on participating policies, which is lawful and not rebating.
distractorExplanations.b: Paying commission to an unlicensed person is a separate licensing violation, not a rebate to the policyowner.
distractorExplanations.c: Inducing replacement through misrepresentation is twisting, not rebating.

life-health-insurance-readiness-check-la.explanation: Rebating gives unfair inducement outside policy contract. It is an unfair trade practice that is unlawful in most states.

options.a: Application/issue for life; at time of loss for property
options.b: Time of loss for life; application/issue for property
options.c: Application/issue and time of loss for both life and property
options.d: Each premium due date for life; at renewal for property

distractorExplanations.b: This reverses the timing: life needs interest at inception, while property needs interest at the time of loss.
distractorExplanations.c: Life insurance does not require insurable interest to continue to the time of death; only property needs it at loss.
distractorExplanations.d: Insurable interest is not re-tested at each premium due date or renewal; the tests are inception (life) and loss (property).

options.a: Created the NAIC to write binding federal model laws
options.b: Leaves insurance regulation primarily to states
options.c: Made insurance regulation a federal duty after SEUA
options.d: Put insurers under the Federal Insurance Office

distractorExplanations.a: The NAIC was formed in 1871 by state regulators, and its model laws bind no one until a state adopts them.
distractorExplanations.c: The 1944 SEUA decision treated insurance as interstate commerce; McCarran-Ferguson (1945) returned regulation to the states.
distractorExplanations.d: The Federal Insurance Office was created by Dodd-Frank in 2010 and monitors the industry; it does not regulate insurers.

life-health-insurance-readiness-check-la.explanation: McCarran-Ferguson preserves state regulation primacy. Federal law applies when it specifically relates to the business of insurance.

options.a: Adds the certificate holder as an insured with full policy rights
options.b: Acts as a temporary contract until the policy is formally issued
options.c: Summarizes coverage for a party but does not amend the policy contract
options.d: Amends policy terms when signed by the agent and the holder

distractorExplanations.a: A certificate does not make the holder an insured; adding an insured requires an endorsement to the policy.
distractorExplanations.b: Temporary coverage until a policy is issued is provided by a binder, not a certificate of insurance.
distractorExplanations.d: Policy terms change only by an insurer-issued endorsement; a certificate signed by the agent amends nothing.

options.a: Insurer knowingly and voluntarily gave up a known right under the policy
options.b: Insured's misstatement on the application was immaterial to underwriting
options.c: Policy has been in force past the two-year contestable period without challenge
options.d: Insurer's actions or statements led insured to reasonably rely to their detriment

distractorExplanations.a: Voluntary relinquishment of a known right is waiver, a sibling doctrine; estoppel rests on the insured's detrimental reliance.
distractorExplanations.b: An immaterial misstatement defeats rescission under misrepresentation rules; it is not the estoppel doctrine.
distractorExplanations.c: Barring contests after two years is the statutory incontestable clause, not equitable estoppel based on insurer conduct.

options.a: Provide privacy notices and safeguard nonpublic personal information
options.b: Obtain opt-in consent before sharing data with any affiliated company
options.c: Give consumers free annual copies of their underwriting credit reports
options.d: Protect health information held by covered health plans and providers

distractorExplanations.b: GLBA uses an opt-out right for sharing with nonaffiliated third parties; it does not require opt-in for affiliates.
distractorExplanations.c: Free annual credit report access comes from the Fair Credit Reporting Act, not from GLBA's privacy rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Protecting health information held by covered plans and providers is the HIPAA Privacy Rule, not GLBA.

options.a: Statistical rates of illness and disability by age and occupation
options.b: Statistical death rates by age and sex among insured populations
options.c: Expected investment earnings used to discount future benefits
options.d: Projected expense loading for commissions and administration

distractorExplanations.a: Rates of illness and disability are morbidity tables, used for health and disability pricing, not mortality tables.
distractorExplanations.c: Expected investment earnings are the interest assumption in pricing, a separate factor from mortality tables.
distractorExplanations.d: Commission and administration costs are the expense loading, a separate pricing factor from mortality.

options.a: Standard premiums with a flat extra for an elevated health risk
options.b: Higher premiums due to a table rating for medical history
options.c: Lower premiums due to favorable health/lifestyle characteristics
options.d: Average premiums reflecting the typical risk in the insured pool

distractorExplanations.a: A flat extra premium is a substandard rating tool for elevated risk, not a feature of the preferred class.
distractorExplanations.b: A table rating with higher premiums describes a substandard (rated) class, not preferred.
distractorExplanations.d: Average premiums for typical risk describe the standard class; preferred risks pay less than standard.

options.a: Coded report of prior application disclosures from the MIB
options.b: Third-party report on the applicant's finances and lifestyle
options.c: Health questionnaire and vitals collected by a paramedical examiner
options.d: Medical records ordered from applicant's doctor for risk assessment

distractorExplanations.a: A coded report of prior application disclosures is an MIB report, not the treating physician's statement.
distractorExplanations.b: A third-party report on finances and lifestyle is an inspection (investigative consumer) report, not an APS.
distractorExplanations.c: Vitals and a questionnaire taken by a paramedical examiner are a paramed exam, not records from the applicant's own doctor.

options.a: Applicant has health conditions increasing mortality risk above standard
options.b: Applicant's risk is below average and qualifies for preferred rates
options.c: Applicant's risk is too high to insure at any premium level
options.d: Applicant joins a group plan issued with no individual health questions

distractorExplanations.b: A below-average risk earns preferred rates; substandard ratings are for risk above standard.
distractorExplanations.c: A risk too high to insure at any price is declined, not issued as a substandard rated policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Guaranteed-issue group enrollment involves no individual risk rating, so no substandard rating is applied.

options.a: Life insurance pricing predicting death rates by age and sex
options.b: Disability and health insurance predicting sickness/injury incidence
options.c: Annuity pricing predicting how long payees will keep living
options.d: Reinsurance pricing predicting catastrophe frequency by region

distractorExplanations.a: Predicting death rates by age and sex uses mortality tables, not morbidity tables.
distractorExplanations.c: Annuity pricing uses annuitant mortality (longevity) tables, not morbidity tables of sickness and injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Regional catastrophe frequency comes from property catastrophe models, not morbidity tables.

options.a: Full medical history ordered from the applicant's physician
options.b: Coded prior application data from the Medical Information Bureau
options.c: Height, weight, blood pressure, blood/urine samples
options.d: Credit and driving record review

distractorExplanations.a: A full history from the applicant's physician is an Attending Physician Statement, not part of the paramed exam.
distractorExplanations.b: Coded prior application data comes from an MIB check, a separate underwriting source from the paramed exam.
distractorExplanations.d: Credit and motor vehicle record checks are separate underwriting reports, not physical measurements taken at a paramed exam.

options.a: Insured changes behavior to take on more risk once coverage is in force
options.b: Insurer selects only the healthiest applicants for coverage
options.c: Losses are spread over a large group of similar, independent exposures
options.d: Higher-risk individuals seek insurance more than lower-risk individuals

distractorExplanations.a: Taking more risk after being covered is moral hazard, a behavioral change, not anti-selection at purchase.
distractorExplanations.b: An insurer picking the healthiest applicants is favorable selection by the insurer, the opposite of anti-selection.
distractorExplanations.c: Spreading losses over many similar exposures is risk pooling (law of large numbers), not anti-selection.

options.a: Transfer portions of risk to another insurer to stabilize capacity
options.b: Transfer its liability to policyowners directly to the reinsurer
options.c: Pool losses with other insurers through a state guaranty association
options.d: Share risk with policyowners through participating dividends

distractorExplanations.b: The ceding insurer stays fully liable to its policyowners; the reinsurer contracts only with the ceding insurer.
distractorExplanations.c: State guaranty associations protect policyowners when an insurer is insolvent; they are not reinsurance.
distractorExplanations.d: Participating dividends return excess premium to owners; they do not transfer risk to another insurer.

options.a: Percentage increase to the standard premium for impaired health
options.b: Fixed dollar charge per policy to cover issue expenses
options.c: Fixed dollar amount per $1,000 of coverage for extra hazard
options.d: Fixed reduction in death benefit for deaths in the first years

distractorExplanations.a: A percentage increase over standard premium is a table rating, not a flat extra per $1,000 of coverage.
distractorExplanations.b: A flat charge per policy for issue costs is a policy fee, not a flat extra for an extra hazard.
distractorExplanations.d: Reducing the death benefit in early years is a graded benefit or lien, not an added flat extra premium.

options.a: Providing full medical records from the applicant's own physicians
options.b: Supplying credit-based insurance scores for rating purposes
options.c: Reporting the applicant's driving history from state DMV files
options.d: Sharing coded prior insurance application history among member insurers

distractorExplanations.a: Full records from the applicant's physicians come from an Attending Physician Statement, not the MIB.
distractorExplanations.b: Credit-based insurance scores come from consumer reporting agencies, not the MIB.
distractorExplanations.c: Driving history comes from a motor vehicle record (MVR) report, not the MIB.

options.a: Driving record, territory, vehicle type, and usage
options.b: Race, religion, and national origin of the vehicle's principal driver
options.c: Mortality and morbidity tables by age and sex
options.d: The applicant's health history from the MIB

distractorExplanations.b: Race, religion, and national origin are unfairly discriminatory factors that insurers may not use in rating.
distractorExplanations.c: Mortality and morbidity tables price life and health coverage, not auto risk classification.
distractorExplanations.d: MIB health history is a life and health underwriting source, not an auto rating factor.

options.a: Insurer issues coverage at a higher premium with a table rating
options.b: Insurer refuses to offer coverage based on risk assessment
options.c: Insurer cancels an in-force policy for nonpayment of premium
options.d: Insurer delays the decision pending an attending physician statement

distractorExplanations.a: Issuing at a higher premium with a table rating is a substandard (rated) offer, not a declination.
distractorExplanations.c: Ending an in-force policy for nonpayment is cancellation or lapse, not an underwriting declination.
distractorExplanations.d: Delaying a decision for more records is a postponement or pending status, not a declination.

options.a: Minimum capital and surplus the state requires the insurer to hold
options.b: Maximum face amount the insurer will issue on any single life
options.c: Maximum loss amount the company keeps before reinsurance applies
options.d: Portion of risk the reinsurer accepts from the ceding company

distractorExplanations.a: Minimum capital and surplus is a statutory solvency requirement, not the retention limit kept before reinsurance.
distractorExplanations.b: The issue limit can exceed retention because the excess is reinsured; retention is what the insurer keeps.
distractorExplanations.d: The portion the reinsurer accepts is the ceded amount, the opposite of what the insurer retains.

options.a: Full coverage from the application date even if the risk is later declined
options.b: Coverage only after the policy is delivered and first premium is paid
options.c: Proof that the agent's underwriting approval binds the insurer
options.d: Limited temporary coverage if premium paid and conditions met

distractorExplanations.a: If the applicant is declined, a conditional receipt provides no coverage; the premium is refunded.
distractorExplanations.b: Delivery-date coverage applies when no premium accompanies the application; a conditional receipt gives interim coverage.
distractorExplanations.c: Life agents cannot bind coverage or approve risks; underwriting approval comes from the insurer.

life-health-insurance-readiness-check-un.explanation: Conditional receipt may cover if death occurs during underwriting if conditions satisfied. Coverage runs pending the underwriting decision.
